tip: Two buts: 'pero' merely contrasts; 'sino' corrects a negative. After 'no solo' it must be 'sino' – and before a full verb like 'baila' it grows a 'que': 'sino que también'.
'Sea cual sea' is literally 'be it which it be' – Spanish wraps the unknown 'destino' in a doubled subjunctive where English gets away with one word: whatever.
'Quedamos' here isn't 'we stayed' – 'quedar' also means to arrange to meet. 'Quedamos a las siete' = we're on for seven; it's the standard verb for making social plans.
Shock is spatial in Spanish: 'no me cabe en la cabeza' uses 'caber', to fit – the outrageous idea literally will not fit inside your head.
English 'if I would have' leaks into Spanish as 'si habría' – banned. 'Si' never takes the conditional: 'si me hubiera levantado' sets the unreal past, 'habría llegado' gives the result.
'Aunque' plays two roles: with 'hubiera' it means 'even IF' (never happened); with plain indicative it's 'even though' (fact). 'Aunque hubiera tenido más tiempo' – that time never existed.
'Caber' means 'to fit', so 'cabe mencionar' is literally 'there's room to mention it' – the polished Spanish move for slipping in a fact worth noting.
'Buenas noches' works coming and going – good evening as a hello after dark, good night as a farewell. One phrase, both directions.
'De nada' = literally 'of nothing' – you owe me nothing, it was nothing. That's the logic inside the Spanish you're-welcome.
Languages go lowercase: 'inglés', never 'Inglés'. Nationalities and days too – Spanish capitalizes far less than English.
In Spain waiters won't bring the bill until you ask – lingering after a meal is normal, not a hint to leave. Say 'la cuenta, por favor', or mime signing in the air.
Why plural? 'Buenos días' wishes you good DAYS – likely from the old blessing 'may God give you good days.' All the time-of-day greetings stay plural.
